title: The written mandala
hookLine: Nichiren's scroll, inscribed with the title and the names of Buddhas

cards: Open the doors of the small cabinet, and there's no statue inside. There's a sheet of paper, mounted as a scroll. Down the middle runs a column of large, bold brushstrokes.
Around it, smaller columns spread toward the edges, like a crowd gathered around a speaker. Some marks near the sides look less like writing than drawing.
People bow to this paper, chant facing it, and dust the cabinet that holds it. The scroll has a name: gohonzon.

teach.b: First, what it is. Gohonzon means, roughly, the object of devotion, said with respect. Nichiren inscribed scrolls like this by hand and gave them to his followers.
Where other temples carved or painted the Buddha, he wrote, which is why some call it a written mandala: a sacred diagram made of words instead of pictures. Second, the center.
Down the middle, in the largest letters, runs yesterday's title, namu myoho renge kyo, with Nichiren's own signature below it. The title is the heart of the scroll, as it is the heart of the chant.
Third, everything around it. The Lotus Sutra tells of a great jeweled tower that rises out of the earth and hangs in the air.
Inside sits a Buddha from an age long past, and Shakyamuni Buddha sits down beside him while a vast assembly gathers to listen.

The gohonzon is often read as that scene, written out: two Buddhas' names on either side of the title, and around them bodhisattvas, disciples, gods and guardians, even beings from the dark and troubled corners of existence.
Even the dark corners have a place on the page. Fourth, how people use it. Practitioners chant facing it, often morning and evening.
Some communities describe it as a kind of mirror: chanting before it, a person is meant to see their own capacity for awakening reflected back.
Communities differ, sometimes deeply, about which scrolls are authentic and who may give them out, and that's tomorrow.
But the scroll is handled with care: kept clean, set up high, never tossed aside.

how: Nichiren Buddhists enshrine a gohonzon, a scroll with the Lotus Sutra's title down the center and the names of Buddhas and other beings around it, and chant facing it, often morning and evening, at home and in temples.

games.q: you're Nichiren. your followers need something to face when they chant. what do you make for them?
o: a carved statue of the Buddha.
a painting of the jeweled tower.
a scroll of written names around the title.
games.why: he writes. the scroll puts the title at the center and the whole assembly of the jeweled tower around it, in words instead of pictures.

practice: Face a sacred scroll, verse or image if there's one where you live, or else any page of writing that matters to you: a letter or a card.
Look at it without reading it, noticing where your eye lands first, what sits at the center and what sits out at the edges.
Then close your eyes, keep the picture in mind, and ask quietly what you would place at the center of your own page.

wordCard.voice: Gohonzon. The scroll Nichiren inscribed, with the Lotus Sutra's title down the center and the names of Buddhas and many beings around it, faced in chanting. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the scroll. Words, not a statue, at the center of the room. Same time tomorrow.
